title: Trees: Build From Preorder and Inorder
oneLiner: Rebuild a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals: preorder names each root, inorder splits the rest into left and right subtrees.
keyTakeaway: The first value in preorder is the root. Its position in inorder splits inorder into the left subtree (everything before it) and the right subtree (everything after). Recurse left first, then right, consuming preorder from the front as you go. A value-to-index map makes each lookup O(1), so the whole build is O(n).
explanation:
preorder and inorder are two traversals of the same binary tree with distinct values. Build the tree and return its root. The grader prints your tree in level order with null for missing children, so for preorder [3, 9, 20, 15, 7] and inorder [9, 3, 15, 20, 7] the answer is [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7].

Recall the orders from Binary Tree Inorder Traversal: preorder visits node, left, right; inorder visits left, node, right. So preorder[0] is the root, 3. In inorder, everything left of 3 ([9]) is the left subtree and everything right of it ([15, 20, 7]) is the right subtree. The same holds inside each subtree, which is the recursion.

Write build(lo, hi), meaning "build the subtree whose values are inorder[lo..hi]". If lo > hi, return null. Otherwise take the next unused value from preorder (keep a running index), make it the node, find its position m in inorder, then build the left child from (lo, m - 1) and the right child from (m + 1, hi). Left must be built before right, because that is the order preorder lists them.

Searching inorder for each root is O(n) per node and O(n²) overall on a skewed tree. Put every value's inorder index in a hash map first and each lookup becomes O(1): O(n) time, O(n) space for the map plus O(h) recursion. This needs distinct values; with duplicates the split point is ambiguous and the tree is not unique.

Preorder alone cannot rebuild a tree: [1, 2] could be 2 as the left or the right child. Inorder pins down the left/right split. Postorder plus inorder works the same way, taking roots from the back of postorder and building right before left.

The visualization rebuilds [3, 9, 20, 15, 7] / [9, 3, 15, 20, 7] one node at a time.

visualizationSteps.message: preorder [3, 9, 20, 15, 7], inorder [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]. Each preorder value is the next root; inorder says what falls to its left and right.
Next in preorder is 3: make it the root of inorder[0..4]. It sits at inorder index 1, so its left subtree is [9] and its right subtree is [15, 20, 7].
Next in preorder is 9: make it the root of inorder[0..0]. It sits at inorder index 0, so its left subtree is nothing and its right subtree is nothing.
Next in preorder is 20: make it the root of inorder[2..4]. It sits at inorder index 3, so its left subtree is [15] and its right subtree is [7].
Next in preorder is 15: make it the root of inorder[2..2]. It sits at inorder index 2, so its left subtree is nothing and its right subtree is nothing.
Next in preorder is 7: make it the root of inorder[4..4]. It sits at inorder index 4, so its left subtree is nothing and its right subtree is nothing.
Every preorder value was used once, in order. Level order: [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7].

pythonHarnessPreamble:
null = None

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def build_level_order_tree(values):
    # Builds a tree from a level-order list; null (None) marks a missing child.
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(values[0])
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    i = 1
    while head < len(queue) and i < len(values):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if values[i] is not None:
            node.left = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(values) and values[i] is not None:
            node.right = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root

def tree_to_list(root):
    # The tree as a level-order list with None for missing children, trailing Nones trimmed.
    result = []
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if node is None:
            result.append(None)
            continue
        result.append(node.val)
        queue.append(node.left)
        queue.append(node.right)
    while result and result[-1] is None:
        result.pop()
    return result
recognitionSignals: Two traversals of a tree are given and you must reconstruct it.
A sequence where the first (or last) element is a root that splits the rest into two ranges, recursively.
gotchas: Building the right subtree before the left consumes preorder values in the wrong order.
Searching inorder linearly for every root is O(n²); precompute a value-to-index map.
Slicing new arrays at every call also costs O(n²) in copying; pass index bounds instead.
confusableWith: Serialize and Deserialize a Binary Tree rebuilds from ONE traversal because it records the null children explicitly; here no nulls are given, so you need two orders.
Convert Sorted Array to a BST picks the middle element as each root; here preorder dictates the roots.

complexity.note: Each of the n values becomes a node once, and the hash map makes each inorder lookup O(1). Space is the map and the tree, O(n), plus O(h) recursion. Without the map, searching inorder for every root is O(n²) on a skewed tree.

referenceSolutions.python:
def build_tree(preorder, inorder):
    index_of = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}  # O(1) splits
    next_pre = 0

    def build(lo, hi):
        nonlocal next_pre
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        node = TreeNode(preorder[next_pre])
        next_pre += 1
        m = index_of[node.val]
        node.left = build(lo, m - 1)  # left first: preorder lists the left subtree next
        node.right = build(m + 1, hi)
        return node

    return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)
